Glacier thickness, thermal regime, and human error
estimation from radio-echo sounding of 25 Svalbard glaciers

text.tspan: Glacier thickness is an essential variable for past, present and future understanding of
glacier dynamics. While thickness inversion methods have gained popularity in recent
years (e.g. Fürst et al., 2018; Millan et al., 2022; van Pelt & Frank, 2025), they still require
measured data for calibration, and are biased to perform well on glacier types similar
to the measured data. In addition, thermal regime (water-content of the ice) is not
explicitly accounted for, leading to potential errors in translating inversion-derived flow
parameters to glaciers of a different thermal regime. Here, we present new Ground
Penetrating Radar (GPR) data from 25 glaciers in Svalbard (Figure 1), adding 707 km to
the ~10000 km (about +7%) of recent data in the Glacier Thickness Database (GlaThiDa).
In addition, our dataset includes thermal regime information, allowing for its use in
assessing glaciological questions and to test model performance.
Glacier GPR measurement uncertainty defines the subsequent use-cases of the method. Lapazaran et al. (2016) provide an excellent overview of sources of error due

tspan.tspan: to instrument limitations. They show that modern systems generally fall in the <2 m uncertainty range, depending on radar performance, positioning uncertainty
and center frequency of the antenna. A source of error that was explicitly beyond the scope of their study, however, was the effect of human interpretation. Do

text.tspan: instrument errors even matter if we cannot interpret the data consistently? We set out to try to answer this question and compare its influence with instrument
errors of Laparazan et al., (2016).
Figure 1. Location of the surveyed glaciers in Svalbard (a), showing insets for b: glaciers in Nathorst Land, c: in Nordaustlandet, and d: in Nordenskiöld

Figure 4. Cross-track differences for all radargrams within the same year. a: differences
for all data, b: differences on a temperate bed (>10% temperate ice), and c: differences
on a cold bed (<10% temperate ice). d: Cross-track differences of the upper boundary
marking of the temperate ice. e: Bootstrapped relationship (black line is the median)
between the columnar temperate ice fraction and bed picking variability.
Figure 5. Glacier thickness measurements compared to previously published data in the Glacier
Thickness Database (GlaThiDa) at points where previous data overlap. The measurements are
grouped by age, and statistics (median±NMAD) for each group are presented. The black line
corresponds to a 1:1 ratio. Note that positive offsets (higher thickness values in GlaThiDa) are
expected if the data are old due to glacier recession; the figure rather shows the
representativeness of these values to today’s state. Point color indicates point density (by a
Gaussian kernel density estimate), with brighter colors showing a larger overlap of points.
Figure 2. Processing workflow summarising the methodology of the study.

Examples of individual radargram interpretations and the final stacked results. a: Radargram from Ragna-Mariebreen showing glacier bed and temperate
ice reflections. b: All subsequent interpretations by users. Note the disparity in interpretations before the 5000 trace mark; some map temperate ice (red lines) while
others say there is none (blue lines). c: stacked result showing the median thickness (black line), temperate ice (red line), and the 25%/75% percentiles in lighter
colors. d, e, f: Example of a cold bed from the ice cap Amenfonna. g, h, i: Example at Drønbreen, e.g. showing a missing bed consensus. j, k, l: Example at

We have gotten fantastic support from the
cryospheric community with interpreting
radargrams! We are about 3/4 there and we
need additional help!
If you want to contribute to a good cause, or

https://radar.mannerfelt.org
We provide new thickness and thermal regime estimates for 707 km of
tracks over 25 glaciers in Svalbard, and we combine consistency tests with
comparisons to other data.
The cross-track differences (Figure 4) reveals a high internal consistency;
two overlapping tracks are generally closer together than the assumed
instrument uncertainty (~2 m). Upper temperate ice boundary
measurements are surprisingly consistent, and there is no clear
relationship between temperate ice fraction and bed picking uncertainty.
Comparing our new thickness data with previous GlaThiDa entries reveals a
high consistency for recent data (2010-), but older data seem less aligned.
A positive bias is assumed, as glacier thinning is not accounted for, but the
spread in both directions is more concerning. Thus, we advise caution for
the use of old data (esp. -1990) as representative of today's thickness.
Our crowd-sourcing experiment has revealed multiple interesting details
about radar interpretation. First, people are very consistent (~1 m) when
it comes to glacier bed picking. However, there are exceptions of systematic
disagreement. Temperate ice thresholding is a clear issue where
contributors disagree on "how much scattering is enough" (Figure 3a-c).
Double bed reflectors create a bimodal distribution in bed picks, and when
to consider the glacier bed invisible is inconsistent (Figure 3j-l).
For future radar efforts, our data support that most radargrams can be
picked reliably by one person. However, areas with unclear indications or
thresholds may vary substaintially between interpreters. Therefore, we
recommend comparing interpretations with colleagues in all unclear cases.
Our study reveals certainties and uncertainties from new radar data
from 25 glaciers in Svalbard. Below is a list of important take-home
messages:
- Radar interpretation is subjective: confer with
colleagues in difficult situations.
- Old (-1990) GlaThiDa measurements may not be
representative of today's geometries.
- Glacier thickness inversion performance
depends on glacier thermal regime.
- Our new data will be available to download
soon!
Figure 6. Glacier thickness measurements compared to thickness models.
The black line corresponds to a 1:1 ratio. Positive median offsets represent a
model overestimation. Point color indicates point density (by a Gaussian
kernel density estimate), with brighter colors showing a larger overlap of
points.
Figure 7. Glacier centerline profiles. Blue is cold ice and red is temperate ice.
a-d have an 8× vertical exaggeration, and e-j have a 12× vertical exaggeration.

text.tspan: Figure 8. Thickness inversion model performance under different thermal conditions. A
positive difference means a model overestimation. There is a clear difference in model
estimation if the glacier is temperate or not, but the bias is not in a consistent direction
between models. This supports that thermal regime is important to incorporate (if data
are available) for future model runs.
We obtained the new GPR data between 2019 and 2025 primarily by snowmobile.
The data were collected at velocities between 10 and 15 km/h with center
frequencies of 100MHz, 25 MHz, and 50 MHz. This is a data compilation of many
field campaigns with different purposes; there is no consistent acquisition plan
(centerlines, zigzags, grids, etc.).
Figure 2 summarizes our data workflow. We process all data in the open software
rsgpr (created by Erik S. Mannerfelt) using ArcticDEMs from similar years for
elevation correction. Then, we upload the radargrams to a custom-made website
for crowd-sourcing interpretations.
Our interpretation crowd-sourcing has been available for qualified contributors
since April 2025. As of this moment, we have had more than 20 active
contributors and we hope for more before completion of the project. Our current
assessment is that roughly eight contributions for each radargram is enough for
a good consensus, but this value may change.
We estimate a consensus (median and spread statistics) from all contributions
(Figure 3), and at a resolution of 5 m per point. These points provide the basis for
the entire rest of the analysis.
We test the performance of thickness inversion models at our survey tracks (Figure 6). It
reveals a rough 1:1 agreement in all cases, but with varying performance statistics. Note that
Fürst et al., (2018) and Farinotti et al., (2019) are similar because the latter is a consensus
estimate that uses the former (and other models). All models tend to overestimate thickness
at low measured values; it might be an artefact of timing-sensitive product such as glacier
outlines.
We observe many different thermal regime configurations. Figure 7 shows ten examples of
configurations in our data. Our hope is that these profiles, combined with future data
collection and archival data publication, will reveal patterns to empirically predict thermal
regime in the near-future. Figure 8 reveals the consequence of not having these data
available for inversion; each model performs differently in cold and temperate ice.
https://github.com/erikmannerfelt/rsgpr
